question.:question/problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)={e}^{y}\,i+{e}^{x}\,j$ across the ellipse $C$ with equation $4{x}^{2}+25{y}^{2}=100.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $5$ and $2,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
r(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={e}^{y}={e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}, \\ Q(x,y) & ={e}^{x}={e}^{5\operatorname{cos}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitutions $u=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,du=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,dt$ and $v=5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,dv=-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,dt,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t})\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-({e}^{5\operatorname{cos}⁡t})\cdot (-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t})\cdot (2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t-{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({e}^{5\operatorname{cos}⁡t})\cdot (-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{0}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u+{\int }_{1}^{1}{e}^{v}\,\text{d}v \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The curve $C$ is given by $x={e}^{y}$ from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(e,1).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $F(x,y)={y}^{2}\,i+\frac{1}{x}\,j$ through $C,$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x={e}^{t}\,y=t,\,t\in [0,1].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(e,1).$ Therefore, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](images/ba/ba6285008fd90835fdbf73203b76a0a01d713889d9939979aaec54bebd0a8c49.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={y}^{2}={t}^{2}, \\ Q(x,y) & =\frac{1}{x}={e}^{-t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})={e}^{t}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2})\cdot (1)-({e}^{-t})\cdot ({e}^{t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}-1\,\text{d}t \\  & =(\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}-t){|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{3}-1)-0 \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $n$ on $C$ is given by

$$

$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $n$ *must* be a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x=t,\,y=\frac{1}{t},\,t\in [\frac{1}{2},2].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(\frac{1}{2},2)$ to the point $(2,\frac{1}{2}).$ Therefore, $n$ is indeed a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation of $T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](images/cc/cc9d66f800a57f27673577cd3fd179b4cd6ff64585c5dc1a867317d8d592e485.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & ={x}^{2}y=t, \\ Q(x,y) & =-y=-\frac{1}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}\left(\frac{1}{t}\right)=-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}(t)\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\right)-\left(-\frac{1}{t}\right)\cdot (1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1/2}^{2}0\,\text{d}t \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨{x}^{2}-{y}^{2},\,{y}^{2}-{z}^{2},\,{z}^{2}⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by $z=-x-y$ for $-2\le x\le 2$ and $-2\le y\le 2.$ Using the parametrization $x=u$ and $y=v,$ the flux of $F$ through $S$ can be expressed as

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={\int }_{-2}^{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}\boxed{}\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.
$$

What is the missing expression?
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,-u-v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,-2\le u\le 2,\,-2\le v\le 2\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(-u-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(-u-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨{x}^{2}-{y}^{2},\,{y}^{2}-{z}^{2},\,{z}^{2}⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=-u-v} \\  & =⟨{u}^{2}-{v}^{2},\,{v}^{2}-(-u-v)^{2},\,(-u-v)^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨{u}^{2}-{v}^{2},\,{v}^{2}-(-u-v)^{2},\,(-u-v)^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =({u}^{2}-{v}^{2})\cdot (1)+({v}^{2}-(-u-v)^{2})\cdot (1)+(-u-v)^{2}\cdot 1 \\  & ={u}^{2}-{v}^{2}+{v}^{2}-(-u-v)^{2}+(-u-v)^{2} \\  & ={u}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨{x}^{2}-{y}^{2},\,{y}^{2}-{z}^{2},\,{z}^{2}⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}{u}^{2}\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

For a surface $S$ given by $z={x}^{2}y$ for $(x,y)\in D,$ the flux of the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}(\bbox[3pt,border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{A}}\,xy+\bbox[3pt,border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{A}}\,{x}^{2}+R)\,\text{d}A.
$$

From left to right, what are the missing parts of the formula?

$$

$$

Since our surface $S$ is of the form $z={x}^{2}y,$ it can be parameterized as

$$

$$

$$

$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x+z,\,2z,\,y+z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by $z=x-3y$ for $-1\le x\le 2$ and $-1\le y\le 3.$ Using the parametrization $x=u$ and $y=v,$ the flux of $F$ through $S$ can be expressed as

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{3}\boxed{}\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.
$$

What is the missing expression?
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,u-3v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 2,\,-1\le v\le 3\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u-3v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u-3v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -3\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,3,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨x+z,\,2z,\,y+z⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=u-3v} \\  & =⟨u+u-3v,\,2(u-3v),\,v+u-3v⟩ \\  & =⟨2u-3v,\,2u-6v,\,u-2v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨2u-3v,\,2u-6v,\,u-2v⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,3,\,1⟩ \\  & =(2u-3v)\cdot (-1)+(2u-6v)\cdot (3)+(u-2v)\cdot 1 \\  & =-2u+3v+6u-18v+u-2v \\  & =5u-17v.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨z-y,\,2y-z,\,xy⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(5u-17v)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{3}(5u-17v)\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Consider the scalar field $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-2{y}^{3}.$ Calculate $$
\displaystyle {\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r,
$$ where $C$ is any smooth path from $(-4,1)$ to $(0,-2)$ in ${R}^{2}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a piecewise-smooth curve given by the vector-valued function $r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b].$ Let $f$ be a differentiable function of two or three variables such that $∇f$ is continuous on $C.$ The fundamental theorem for line integrals states that 

$$
{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r=f(r(b))-f(r(a)).
$$

 

This theorem implies that the line integral of a conservative vector field depends only on the value of $f$ at the initial and terminal points $A$ and $B,$ and is independent of the path between them.

In our case, the coordinates of the endpoints of the path $C$ are $A(-4,1)$ and $B(0,-2).$

Applying the fundamental theorem for line integrals, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}∇f\cdot \text{d}r & =f(0,-2)-f(-4,1) \\  & =({0}^{2}-2(-2)^{3})-((-4)^{2}-2(1)^{3}) \\  & =16-16+2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that $\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F$ denotes the divergence of the vector field $F.$

Intuitively, the divergence of $F$ at a point $P$ measures how much $F$ acts like a source or a sink at $P:$

- If $F$ acts like a source at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F>0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F<0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like neither a source nor a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F=0$ at $P.$

If $∇\cdot F=0$ everywhere in the domain of $F,$ we say that $F$ is solenoidal.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement:

- Statement $∇\cdot F>0$ is true, whereas statements $∇\cdot F=0$ and $∇\cdot F<0$ are false. Notice that the lengths of the vector's $y$-components increase as we move vertically away from the origin. Therefore, the vector field $F$ acts like a source at every point.

- Statement “$F$ is solenoidal” is false. Since $∇\cdot F\ne 0,$ the vector field $F$ is not solenoidal.

Therefore, the correct answer is $∇\cdot F>0$ only.

$$

$$

$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\sqrt{(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{3}\sqrt{{r}^{2}}\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{3}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[\frac{{r}^{3}}{3}]}_{1}^{3}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(9-\frac{1}{3})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{26}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{26}{3}[\theta ]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{26}{3}\cdot 2\pi  \\  & =\frac{52\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}

$$

we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y \\  & ={∮}_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r\end{aligned}
$$

$\frac{∂P}{∂y}={e}^{x}$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1-{e}^{x},$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-2{e}^{x}\ne 1.
$$

$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2$
and
$\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1,$
which gives

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-1\ne 1.
$$

$\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-\frac{1}{3}$

$$

$$

Calculate $$
\displaystyle {∮}_{∂D}({x}^{2}-{y}^{4})\,dx+({x}^{3}y-x{y}^{3})\,dy,
$$ where $D$ is the annular region shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{4}$ and $Q(x,y)=({x}^{3}y-x{y}^{3}).$ So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-4{y}^{3},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}y-{y}^{3}.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}({x}^{2}-{y}^{4})\,dx+({x}^{3}y-x{y}^{3})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3{x}^{2}y-{y}^{3}-(-4{y}^{3})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3{x}^{2}y+3{y}^{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3y({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 4,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

Recall that the change of variables formula for polar coordinates gives

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, our double integral becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}3y({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{4}3\cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot ((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{4}3{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot {r}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{4}3{r}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{1}^{4}3{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi }\cdot \frac{3{r}^{5}}{5}\,{|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))\cdot (\frac{3(4)^{5}}{5}-\frac{3(1)^{5}}{5}) \\  & =(1-1)\cdot (\frac{3(4)^{5}}{5}-\frac{3(1)^{5}}{5}) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$
